name: Vomit Cake (aka Magic Cookie Bars)
flags: Family-named version credited to Rob Hopcke. The dish descends from the Eagle Brand Magic Cookie Bars (1963), but quantities and method differ materially: family uses 1 stick butter / 1 c graham crumbs / 1 c coconut / 1 c chips / 1 c walnuts / 15 oz condensed milk drizzled last, vs Eagle Brand's 1/2 c butter / 1.5 c crumbs / 14 oz milk poured over the crust first / 2 c (12 oz) chips / 1-1/3 c coconut. Not the same recipe, so no link recorded. Runner-up a human could promote: https://www.eaglebrand.com/recipe/magic-cookie-bars/

name: White Sauce
flags: Unattributed thin/medium/thick bechamel ratio table (1 c milk with 1, 2 or 3 T each flour and butter). This is a generic kitchen-reference ratio printed in dozens of mid-century American cookbooks; no single published page can be identified as the source. Nearest generic equivalents: https://www.bettycrocker.com/recipes/basic-white-sauce-recipe/f610bfaf-e83b-4243-997b-ec16b8f5e155 and https://www.tasteofhome.com/recipes/basic-white-sauce/ — neither should be recorded as the origin.

name: Whoopie Pies
flags: Family source (Aunt Debby). One confirming search run: the Crisco-cake / Crisco-plus-Fluff-filling formula is the standard New England church-cookbook whoopie pie, and the family proportions (6 T Crisco, 5 T cocoa, 3/4 c Crisco + 3/4 c confectioners sugar + 6 heaping T Fluff in the filling) do not match any published version found. Closest published relatives, not the source: https://marshmallowfluff.com/whoopie-pies/ and https://newengland.com/food/desserts/homemade-whoopie-pies-3/

name: Butterscotch Pudding
flags: Identified with confidence as Melissa Clark's Butterscotch Pudding for The New York Times - the family text matches word for word, including the dual US/metric ingredient list (3/4 packed cup/165 grams dark brown sugar; 2 cups/480 milliliters whole milk; 1 cup/240 milliliters heavy cream) and the closing tip about bringing the pudding to a full vigorous boil to activate the cornstarch. cooking.nytimes.com returned SITE_BLOCKED on fetch, so no URL recorded and no digest built. Attribution independently confirmed by https://thebrookcook.wordpress.com/2021/03/09/butterscotch-pudding/ which reprints it as 'adapted from The New York Times, Melissa Clark' - a human could promote that reprint, or the NYT original once unblocked. Gram weights already present in the family copy: dark brown sugar 165 g, milk 480 ml, cream 240 ml.

name: Cauliflower Soup
headnote: Dan Souza for Cook's Illustrated / America's Test Kitchen. The trick is staggering the cauliflower: part of the head goes into the pot early and part late, so the finished soup carries both the sweet, deeply cooked flavour and the fresher, grassier note of briefly cooked florets. Cauliflower has enough body of its own that pureeing it with water alone gives a velvety texture, so no cream is needed. A separate handful of florets is browned in butter and used, with the resulting brown butter, as the garnish.
comment_digest: NO COMMENTS returned on the recipe page.
flags: Verified line by line against the family copy: 2 lb head cauliflower, 8 tbsp butter in 8 pieces, 1 leek (white and light green, halved, sliced thin, washed), 1 small onion halved and sliced thin, 4-5 cups water, 1/2 tsp sherry vinegar, 3 tbsp minced chives - identical, including the unusual 1/2 tsp sherry vinegar and the 3 tbsp chives. Family copy carried no source line; ATK/Cook's Illustrated confirmed. Companion article: https://www.americastestkitchen.com/cooksillustrated/articles/6643-creamy-cauliflower-soup

name: Croque Monsieur
headnote: Alton Brown's take on the French ham-and-cheese, published on his own site as 'Mr. Crunchy.' The sandwich is built open-faced so the broiler can do two jobs at once: melt the Gruyere and crisp the bread's surface. A roux-based bechamel seasoned with thyme, white pepper and nutmeg is spread over the ham so the sandwich stays moist under high heat, and a homemade herbes de Provence blend goes on top. Add a fried egg and it becomes a croque madame.
comment_digest: NO COMMENTS on the page.
flags: Bechamel matches the family copy exactly - 2 Tbsp butter, 1 oz flour, 8 oz whole milk, 1 tsp fresh thyme, 1/2 tsp kosher salt, 1/2 tsp white pepper, 1/4 tsp grated nutmeg - as do the 4 half-inch sourdough slices and 1 Tbsp whole grain mustard. Only difference is the fillings: the site version says 6 oz Gruyere / 4 oz ham / 1 tsp herbes, the family copy 8 oz each and 2 tsp herbes; that is the cookbook-vs-website variance, same author, same recipe. The site also gives the full herbes de Provence blend the family copy assumes you have: 1 Tbsp each dried thyme, rosemary, tarragon, basil; 2 tsp each fennel seed and marjoram; 1 tsp each oregano, dill, chervil.

name: Mushroom Stroganoff
headnote: Alton Brown, excerpted from Alton Brown: EveryDayCook. His argument is that beef was never essential to stroganoff - noodles and sour cream are the Russian part, and mushrooms belong there at least as much as beef does. Searing the portobellos in two batches rather than crowding the pan is what builds the dark fond the flour and broth later deglaze, and goat cheese stirred in with the sour cream adds the tang and body that beef fat would otherwise supply.
comment_digest: NO COMMENTS on the page.
flags: Exact ingredient match to the family copy, quantity for quantity: 10 oz extra wide egg noodles, 2 Tbsp unsalted butter, 5 portobellos (stems and gills removed, thinly sliced), 1 tsp kosher salt, 10 scallions, 1 Tbsp AP flour, 14 oz beef broth, 1 cup sour cream, 4 oz goat cheese, 1/2 tsp black pepper. The family copy's 'Cold Water Pasta, see M' cross-reference confirms the EveryDayCook book text. tastecooking.com is a licensed excerpt; note altonbrown.com hosts only a different 'Mushroom Stroganoff Toast' (https://altonbrown.com/recipes/mushroom-stroganoff-toast/), which is NOT this recipe.

name: Lahey Stecca
rating: 5 out of 5 stars (vote count not shown)
headnote: Jim Lahey's stick loaves from My Bread, run by Leite's Culinaria as a licensed excerpt. The no-knead method does the work: a 10-to-18-hour room-temperature ferment with a quarter teaspoon of yeast develops the flavour and gluten that kneading would otherwise have to build. Because the loaves are stretched thin, they bake through in 15 to 25 minutes at 500F rather than needing a covered pot, and the olive oil and coarse salt brushed on before the second rise give the crust its snap.
comment_digest: Testers warn the tips brown fast, so watch the last few minutes. Plan roughly 20 hours from start to table. Double the batch for six or more - it goes quickly. Several preferred the loaves plain with just olive oil and coarse salt rather than topped, which matches Robert's own cook's note that he almost never adds the garlic, olives or tomatoes.
flags: Exact match to the family copy: 3 cups bread flour, 1/2 tsp table salt, 3/4 tsp sugar, 1/4 tsp instant or active dry yeast, 1 1/2 cups cool 55-65F water, 1/4 cup EVOO, 3/4 tsp coarse salt, about 20 topping pieces (5 per loaf), 4 loaves. Gram note: the family copy already carries weights the published page lacks - 400 g bread flour and 350 g water, i.e. an 87.5 percent hydration by the family's own reckoning (350/400). Alternate full text: https://steamykitchen.com/6795-no-knead-baguette-stecca.html

name: Model Bakery English Muffins
headnote: From The Model Bakery Cookbook (Chronicle, 2013) by Karen and Sarah Mitchell with Rick Rodgers, reprinted on Bakepedia. Hand-shaping the muffins instead of baking them in ring molds turned out to give bigger, airier muffins - better for sandwiches - so the book abandoned the bakery's own original method. A biga made 12 to 24 hours ahead supplies the flavour and structure, and the muffins are cooked on a cast-iron griddle in clarified butter rather than baked.
comment_digest: Dense muffins trace to under-proofing, the wrong flour, or tired yeast. Griddle heat is the step people get wrong - keep it to medium, around 275F. Two tablespoons of clarified butter per batch is enough despite the 6 Tbsp the recipe allows. The 1/4 tsp yeast in the biga looks too low but is correct as printed. High-altitude bakers need adjustments.
flags: Exact match to the family copy including the published gram/millilitre weights: biga 1/2 cup/75 g bread flour + 1/4 cup/60 ml water + 1/4 tsp instant yeast; dough 1 1/3 cups/315 ml water, 3/4 tsp instant yeast, 1 Tbsp plus 1 tsp EVOO, 1 1/2 tsp fine sea salt, 3 1/2 cups/510 g unbleached AP flour; plus 1/4 cup/35 g yellow cornmeal and 6 Tbsp/90 ml clarified butter. The family copy's step-2 sub-weight (3 cups/435 g of the flour) also matches. Robert's cook's note - cornmeal on both sides, cast iron, clarified butter - is consistent with the published method.

name: Kung Pao Chicken With Peanuts (Gong Bao Ji Ding)
headnote: Fuchsia Dunlop's Sichuan gong bao, reprinted by Leite's Culinaria. The chicken is marinated in potato flour, soy and Shaoxing so it stays tender through the brief, very hot stir-fry - the coating is the whole point. The sauce is mixed in advance because once the wok is going there is no time; its balance of sugar, Chinkiang black vinegar and two soy sauces is what separates the real dish from takeout. Whole dried chillies and Sichuan pepper are fried first, for fragrance rather than raw heat.
comment_digest: Cut the chillies back if you want it mild - leaving them whole lets heat-averse eaters pick them out, and heat varies a lot by chilli type. Arrowroot works as a substitute for the potato flour. A nonstick pan keeps the sauce from catching better than stainless. One cook finished it with angel hair pasta and liked it.
flags: Marinade and sauce match the family copy ingredient for ingredient: marinade 1/2 tsp salt, 2 tsp light soy, 1 tsp Shaoxing, 1 1/2 tsp potato flour, 1 Tbsp water; sauce 1 Tbsp (family: 3 tsp) sugar, 3/4 tsp potato flour, 1 tsp dark soy, 1 tsp light soy, 1 Tbsp (family: 3 tsp) Chinkiang vinegar, 1 tsp sesame oil, 1 Tbsp stock. Chicken 2/3 lb vs family's 300 g / 3/4 lb; 10+ dried chillies, 1 tsp Sichuan pepper, 2/3 cup (family: 75 g) roasted peanuts, 3 garlic, equal ginger, 5 spring onions - all the same. Gram anchors usable for conversion: roasted peanuts 2/3 cup = 75 g; chicken breast 300 g = 2 breasts.

name: Chicken Thighs With Anchovy, Caper And Garlic
flags: No source line in the family copy; archived 2013-10-30. The text reads like a New York Times / Melissa Clark recipe (heat oven to 400, build an anchovy-garlic-caper oil, brown thighs, finish with minced garlic and the juice of half a lemon), and cooking.nytimes.com returns SITE_BLOCKED so that hypothesis could not be tested. Every candidate found is by an unrelated author and none matches: Domestic Dreamboat (https://domesticdreamboat.com/chicken-thighs-with-anchovies-and-capers/) is close in spirit - 6 garlic, 5 anchovies, 2 T capers, chile flakes, lemon, parsley - but carries no attribution and uses 2 lb chicken and 2 T oil against the family's 1 1/4 lb and 1/4 cup; Well Seasoned Studio (https://www.wellseasonedstudio.com/anchovy-chicken/) is a different method. Deliberately not linked - a human with NYT access should check for a Melissa Clark original before promoting anything.

name: Deviled Eggs
flags: Robert's own recipe and his own first-person note (2013 'Deviled Eggs recipez' message). The signature ingredients - Durkee sauce, Wickles relish, toasted-and-ground mustard seed alongside yellow deli mustard - are a personal formula, not a published one. One confirming search run; no published recipe combines these. No link recorded.

name: Everyday Turmeric Chicken Drumsticks
headnote: Naz Deravian, from Bottom of the Pot: Persian Recipes and Stories - the dish is morgh ba zardchoobeh, her family's weeknight standby. Slitting the drumsticks is the working part of the technique: it shortens the cooking and lets the turmeric, salt and lemon reach the meat rather than sitting on the skin-less surface. The onion is cooked down to gold first so its sweetness balances turmeric's earthiness, and the sauce is finished with lemon juice and a scant quarter cup of hot water rather than stock, which keeps it bright.
comment_digest: Readers questioned whether the full 2 1/2 tsp kosher salt is right if the chicken was already koshered (i.e. pre-salted) - worth halving in that case. Several cooked the drumsticks noticeably longer than the stated 35 minutes.
flags: Identical to the family copy, quantity for quantity: 10 skinless drumsticks (about 3 lb), 1 tsp ground turmeric, 2 1/2 tsp kosher salt, 1/4 tsp black pepper, 3 Tbsp olive oil, 1 medium yellow onion diced, 2 cloves garlic, optional splash of white wine, 2 Tbsp lemon juice, parsley. The family copy's MAKE AHEAD / PLAN AHEAD blocks and the line 'taste as it cooks and make delicious' are Deravian's own. kosher.com is a licensed reprint of the cookbook, not the author's site; the author's own site is https://bottomofthepot.com/ but does not host this recipe.

name: Flour Bakery Chocolate Chip Cookies
headnote: Joanne Chang of Flour Bakery, Boston. She hand-chops bar chocolate instead of using chips, both so you can pick the chocolate and so the shards give bigger, more irregular pockets than uniform chips do. The dough is built on a mix of bread flour and all-purpose - the bread flour's extra protein gives the chew - and she insists on chilling it overnight, which hydrates the flour and deepens the flavour before baking.
comment_digest: NO COMMENTS shown on the page.
flags: Confirmed as Joanne Chang's Flour chocolate chunk cookie. The distinctive chocolate split matches the family copy to the gram: 9 oz / 250-255 g semisweet chopped (about 1 1/2 cups) plus 2 1/2 oz / 70 g milk chocolate (about 1/2 cup), as do 3/4 cup/150 g granulated, 3/4 cup/165-175 g light brown, 1 cup/224-228 g butter, 2 eggs, 1 tsp baking soda, 1/2 tsp salt. One variance across printings: MasterClass gives 1 cup/150 g bread flour + 1 cup/140 g AP, the family copy 1 cup/160 g bread + 1 1/4 cups/175 g AP - i.e. the family copy runs about 45 g more flour. Gram weights on the published page are usable for the conversion project. Robert's own notes (72 percent cacao too dark, 45 percent not dark enough; 1/2 tsp vanilla per full recipe) are his, not the author's - note the family ingredient list omits vanilla although the method calls for it, while MasterClass lists 1 tsp.

name: Pizza Crust for a Baking Stone or Steel
headnote: Jim Lahey's no-knead pizza dough from My Pizza (with Rick Flaste, Clarkson Potter, 2012), reprinted by the James Beard Foundation. An 18-hour room-temperature ferment on a single gram of yeast does the work kneading would otherwise do: the gluten organises itself and the long rise builds the flavour. The dough is then divided and shaped into four rounds by folding in from four sides, and can be held wrapped in the fridge for up to three days.
comment_digest: NO COMMENTS on the page.
flags: Baker's-percentage match to the family copy exactly: 500 g flour, 1 g active dry yeast, 16 g fine sea salt, 350 g water - 70 percent hydration, 3.2 percent salt. The family copy adds the US equivalents (17 1/2 oz / about 3 3/4 cups flour; 1/4 tsp yeast; 2 tsp salt; 1 1/2 cups water) and Robert's own 4 percent sugar variation for faster browning, which is not in the original. Note Robert's 2026 note that he no longer owns a stone or steel and now bakes these in an Ooni or cast iron. Alternate copies: https://bakingsteel.com/blogs/recipes/jim-laheys-no-knead-dough and https://leitesculinaria.com/89307/recipes-pizza-dough.html

name: Penne Alla Vodka
headnote: Ina Garten's version, on her own Barefoot Contessa site. The unusual move is that the sauce is not simmered on the stove but covered and baked at 375F for an hour and a half, which concentrates the tomatoes without scorching them and needs no attention. The vodka goes in early and is reduced by half before the tomatoes are crushed in by hand, so its bite cooks off and only the aroma it carries remains. The sauce is pureed smooth after baking, then finished with cream, fresh oregano and Parmesan.
comment_digest: NO COMMENTS on the page.
flags: Matches the family copy ingredient for ingredient and step for step: 1/4 cup good olive oil, 2 1/2 cups chopped onion, 1 Tbsp minced garlic (3 cloves), 1 1/2 tsp dried oregano, 1/2 tsp red pepper flakes, 1 cup vodka, 2 (28 oz) cans whole peeled plum tomatoes drained, 3/4 lb penne, 2 Tbsp fresh oregano, 1 cup heavy cream, 1/2 cup Parmesan, plus 2 tsp salt / 1/2 tsp pepper into the pot and 2 Tbsp salt in the pasta water. The only wording difference is the onion - family copy says 'Spanish onion (1 large)', the site 'yellow onions (2 onions)' - a printing variance between her cookbooks, not a different recipe. Printable version: https://barefootcontessa.com/recipes/print/63194

name: Pork Shoulder Ragu
headnote: Andy Ward writing on Jenny Rosenstrach's Dinner: A Love Story, filed under 'Instant Dinner Party.' His point is that the recipe is entertaining strategy as much as cooking: everything happens in the three-to-four-hour braise, so by the time guests arrive the host has nothing left to do. Keeping the braising liquid at about a third of the way up the meat is what lets the shoulder go fork-tender without the sauce turning watery, and the fennel seed and a tablespoon of hot sauce supply the smoky, faintly sausage-like note that makes it read as more work than it was.
comment_digest: A pressure cooker does it in about 30 minutes. It freezes well - readers pack leftovers in quart jars for months. Bone-in shoulder works. The sauce thickens a lot once the meat is shredded back in, so add diced tomatoes or a little liquid to loosen it.
flags: Exact match to the family copy: 2 to 2 1/2 lb boneless pork shoulder, 1 small onion, 1 garlic clove, 2 Tbsp olive oil plus a small pat of butter, 1 large can whole tomatoes with juice, 1 cup red wine, 5 sprigs each thyme and oregano, a small handful of fennel seeds, 1 Tbsp hot sauce, pappardelle, Parmesan; 325F, 3-4 hours, turning hourly. The family copy's scaling note (3 lb pork for eight) is the blog's own. Also reprinted with a review at https://food52.com/recipes/39733-andy-ward-jenny-rosenstrach-s-pork-shoulder-ragu and https://www.thekitchn.com/dinner-a-love-story-slow-braised-pork-ragu-recipe-23115729

name: Giada's Mushroom Ragù
headnote: Giada De Laurentiis, from Everyday Italian. The mushrooms are cooked over high heat until every bit of their liquid has gone, which is what concentrates their flavour instead of stewing them; only then does the Marsala go in, off the heat, and reduce away. A long half-hour reduction of chicken broth builds the body a meat ragu would get from bones, and the Parmesan, basil and parsley go in off the heat at the end. She warns against plain white button mushrooms, which carry too much water and too little flavour.
comment_digest: NO COMMENTS available - Food Network's review panel did not load.
flags: Same recipe family, not provably the exact printing the family copy came from. Family copy: 1 cup Marsala, no cream, 2/3 cup Parmesan, 1/2 tsp salt and 1/4 tsp pepper stated explicitly. Food Network (Everyday Italian): 1/2 cup Marsala plus 1/3 cup heavy cream, 1/2 to 3/4 cup Parmesan. Giadzy, her own site (https://giadzy.com/blogs/recipes/giadas-mushroom-ragu), instead uses 3/4 cup red wine, 2/3 cup Parmesan and 1 Tbsp butter. Everything else - 1/4 cup EVOO, 1 large onion, 2 garlic cloves, 1 lb mixed wild mushrooms, 5 basil leaves, 1/4 cup parsley, 2 cups chicken broth - is identical across all three. Chose the Food Network page because Marsala is the family copy's distinctive ingredient; a human might prefer the Giadzy page as the author's own site. Duplicate FN posting: https://www.foodnetwork.com/recipes/mushroom-ragu-recipe-1956251

name: Melted Caramelized Onions
headnote: Thomas Keller's Melted Onions from Ad Hoc at Home, reproduced on a home cook's blog. The onions are first cooked dry over medium-low heat for about 20 minutes so they give up their own liquid, and only then is a full stick of butter and an aromatic sachet added for another half hour. The point is emulsion rather than browning - the onions should stay creamy-looking throughout, and if the butter breaks or the pan dries, a splash of cold water stirred in brings it back together. The result is meltingly tender onions that still hold their shape.
comment_digest: NO COMMENTS on the post.
flags: Recipe identity is certain - the ingredient list matches the family copy exactly (8 cups sliced onions from about 3 large onions, kosher salt, 8 Tbsp / 1 stick / 4 oz unsalted butter cut in 8 pieces, and a sachet of 1 bay leaf, 3 thyme sprigs, 10 peppercorns, 1 smashed garlic clove), as do the 20-minute and 30-to-35-minute stages, the re-emulsifying trick and the 3-day keep. Confidence held at medium only because this is an unaffiliated blog reprint rather than a publisher's page - no authorised online copy of Ad Hoc at Home's Melted Onions was found. One wording difference: the blog says 'cover' where the family copy and the book specify a parchment lid. Index entry confirming the recipe exists in the book: https://www.eatyourbooks.com/library/recipes/314023/melted-onions

name: Roux
flags: Thomas Keller's basic roux from Ad Hoc at Home (8 Tbsp / 1 stick / 4 oz unsalted butter to 1/2 cup plus 3 Tbsp all-purpose flour - equal parts by weight, about 113 g each). Searched; no authorised or faithful online reproduction of this specific Keller roux was found, only generic roux explainers by other authors (e.g. https://www.thekitchn.com/roux-recipe-23003997), which would be the wrong attribution. Gram note for the conversion project: the recipe is explicitly equal parts butter and flour BY WEIGHT, so 113 g / 113 g; the odd '1/2 cup plus 3 tablespoons' flour measure exists only because a stick of butter weighs more per cup than flour does.

name: Oatmeal Raisin Cookies
headnote: Joanne Chang's Flour Bakery oatmeal raisin cookie, reprinted with commentary by David Lebovitz. Two things do the work: beating the butter and sugars a full five minutes so the dough carries air, and then, counterintuitively, flattening the domed cookies partway through baking - which collapses that air and gives the dense, chewy crumb rather than a cakey one. No vanilla and no water; the spicing is just nutmeg and cinnamon.
comment_digest: Readers routinely swap the raisins for dried cherries, cranberries or apricots, or add chocolate or butterscotch chips and walnuts or pecans. Several confirm the mid-bake flattening genuinely produces a chewier cookie and is worth doing. Cookies that spread flat trace to butter softened in the microwave - it goes past room temperature and the dough slackens. A few found the instructions ambiguous about when the eggs go in.
flags: Matches the family copy on the distinctive numbers: 1 3/4 cups/245 g flour, 1 3/4 cups/175 g old-fashioned oats, 1 1/2 cups/240 g raisins, 1 tsp baking soda, 1 tsp salt, 1/4 tsp freshly grated nutmeg, 2 eggs, 1 cup butter. Minor printing variances: Lebovitz gives 2/3 cup (150 g) granulated where the family copy says 3/4 cup (150 g) - same gram weight, so the gram figure is the reliable one; 1 cup (200 g) brown vs the family's 1 cup (220 g); butter 225 g vs 228 g; and cinnamon 1 tsp vs the family's 1/4 tsp, which is the one real discrepancy worth a human's eye. Licensed cookbook text (paywalled): https://app.ckbk.com/recipe/flou69447c02s001r005/oatmeal-raisin-cookies

name: Xi'an Famous Foods Cumin Lamb
headnote: Jason Wang, from the Xi'an Famous Foods cookbook - the shop's signature dish, which used to sell out before the noodles were even ready. Slicing the lamb paper-thin (easiest when it is partly frozen) maximises the surface the cumin and chilli can cling to, and a light cornstarch coating protects the meat over very high heat. The key instruction is to cook in small batches: crowd the pan and the lamb steams grey instead of browning.
comment_digest: NO COMMENTS on the page.
flags: Exact match to the family copy, including the gram weight the family copy carries: 10 oz (280 g) boneless lamb leg, ideally partially frozen; 1 1/2 tsp cornstarch; 2 tsp plus 2 Tbsp vegetable oil divided; 1 green onion; 1-inch (2.5 cm) ginger; 1 garlic clove sliced; 1 1/2 Tbsp ground cumin; 1 tsp salt; 1 1/2 tsp red chili powder; 1/2 medium red onion sliced; 1 longhorn pepper diagonally sliced. Robert's own note applies directly - if substituting cayenne for the shop's red chili powder, use far less. Publisher's excerpt of the same recipe: https://abramsbooks.tumblr.com/post/632140686025785344/recipe-spicy-cumin-lamb-from-xian-famous-foods

name: Red-Cooked Pork Belly (Hongshao Rou)
headnote: Diana Kuan, adapting Fuchsia Dunlop's Revolutionary Chinese Cookbook. The sugar is caramelised in oil before the pork goes in - that is what gives hongshao rou its mahogany colour and its faint bitterness against the soy. Blanching the belly first firms it enough to cube neatly and rids it of scum. Kuan argues the dish is underrated abroad and points out it is one of the mildest things in the Hunan repertoire, Mao Zedong's favourite; she is emphatic that the skin and fat are most of what makes it good.
comment_digest: The page shows roughly 27 comments but their text did not render on fetch, so no themes could be extracted. Worth a human revisit.
flags: This is the exact source of the family copy. Ingredient list matches item for item (1 lb pork belly, 2 Tbsp peanut oil, 2 Tbsp white sugar, 1 Tbsp Shaoxing, 1-inch ginger sliced, 2 star anise, 2 dried red chilies, 1 cinnamon stick or cassia, 2 Tbsp light soy, salt and sugar to taste, scallion greens) and the family copy's closing line about the skin and fat being 80 percent of what makes hongshao rou good is verbatim from this page - which is why the library's 'Further notes' says the long blurb in the body is the original blogger's headnote.

name: Thomas Keller Egg Yolk Pasta For Two
flags: The family copy is Robert's own arithmetic, not a published recipe: 120 g flour, '5 egg yolks (or 4 2/3)', '0 eggs (or 1/3)', 1/2 tsp EVOO, 1/2 tsp whole milk - the parenthetical thirds are the giveaway that he divided a larger Keller formula by three and then rounded. It does not scale from the French Laundry seven-yolk dough (1 3/4 cups / 8 oz flour, 6 yolks, 1 whole egg, 1 1/2 tsp olive oil, 1 Tbsp milk), which at 120 g of flour would give about 3 yolks, not 5. Deliberately not linked. Runner-up for a human to check against whichever Keller book Robert used: https://smittenkitchen.com/2008/02/seven-yolk-pasta-dough/ (French Laundry dough, fully reprinted) and https://app.ckbk.com/recipe/fren57567c02s001ss004r001/pasta-dough (licensed original).

name: Fresh Pasta For Two
flags: No source in the family copy; three lines long (1 large egg + 1 large egg yolk, 125 g flour, 1/8 tsp salt) with Robert's own thumb test for hydration and an 8-minute hand knead. This is a ratio, not an attributable recipe - one egg plus one yolk to 125 g flour is the common two-portion proportion and appears unattributed across dozens of sites. No published page can be defended as the origin, so nothing recorded.

name: Heston's Slow-Roasted Brined Chicken
headnote: Heston Blumenthal's roast chicken as broadcast in How to Cook Like Heston. Two things carry it: an overnight 6 percent brine, which seasons the bird throughout and helps the muscle hold water, and then a very low 90C oven that takes three to four hours to bring the breast to 60C, so the meat never contracts and squeezes its juices out. The bird rests a full 45 minutes, then goes back into an oven turned as high as it will go for about ten minutes purely to colour the skin - browning is separated from cooking.
comment_digest: NO COMMENTS on the page.
flags: Exact match to the family copy, including the quantities and the safety caveat: 6 percent brine of 300 g salt in 5 litres water; 1.5-2 kg chicken; 1 lemon; 1 bunch thyme; 125 g unsalted butter at room temperature plus extra for the skin; 30 ml dry white wine; optional gravy of 20 ml wine, 250 ml chicken stock, 1 tsp Dijon, a sprig each of tarragon and parsley. Oven 90C (about 70C fan, gas 1/4), roast to 60C internal over 3-4 hours, rest 45 minutes, blast at maximum about 10 minutes; the page carries the same warning that food-safety guidance wants 75C in the thickest part of the breast, which is the line Robert's copy opens with. Note a widely circulated fan version at https://bigspud.co.uk/heston-blumenthals-roast-chicken/ uses a smaller 1.4 kg bird and 240 g salt in 4 litres - not the family's version.

name: Light and Fluffy Pancakes
headnote: Cook's Illustrated's Light and Fluffy Pancakes as printed in The New Best Recipe. The batter uses both baking powder and baking soda, and the acid that activates the soda comes from milk soured with a tablespoon of lemon juice - the test kitchen's tasters actually preferred that to real buttermilk. The batter is whisked only until barely combined and left visibly lumpy, because developing gluten is what makes pancakes tough and flat.
comment_digest: Only one substantive note on the reprint: the cook records that Cook's Illustrated's own tasters preferred the lemon-juice-and-milk mixture over buttermilk. Otherwise NO COMMENTS.
flags: Recipe identity is certain - this reprint matches the family copy line for line, including the unusual details: 1 Tbsp lemon juice, 2 cups milk, 2 cups (10 ounces) unbleached AP flour, 2 Tbsp sugar, 2 tsp baking powder, 1/2 tsp baking soda, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 large egg, 3 Tbsp melted butter, 1-2 tsp vegetable oil, and the note 'If you have buttermilk on hand, use 2 cups instead of the milk and lemon juice mixture.' Confidence held at medium only because this is a home blog rather than the publisher. Caution for whoever promotes this: America's Test Kitchen's own page of the same title, https://www.americastestkitchen.com/recipes/1273-light-and-fluffy-pancakes, is a DIFFERENT and smaller formula (1 cup flour, 3/4 cup buttermilk plus 1/4 cup milk, egg separated, 4.5 stars from 144 ratings) - do not substitute it. Gram anchor from the family copy: 2 cups AP flour = 10 oz = 284 g.

name: Flour Peanut Butter Cookies
headnote: Joanne Chang's peanut butter cookies from Flour: Spectacular Recipes from Boston's Flour Bakery + Cafe, reproduced by a home baker. The dough takes essentially a whole jar of chunky peanut butter, which is what gives the cookie its shortbread-like crumb and a flavour close to eating peanut butter straight. The butter and both sugars are creamed a full five minutes to aerate, the peanut butter goes in after the eggs, and the dough is chilled overnight so it holds its shape through a long bake at a low temperature.
comment_digest: Little discussion beyond the baker's own notes: chill overnight if you can, three to four hours at minimum, and the baked cookies are notably large and not very sweet. One reader suggested them as ice-cream sandwich shells.
flags: Gram weights match the family copy exactly: 1 cup (228 g) unsalted butter, 1 cup (200 g) granulated, 1 cup (220 g) packed light brown, 2 eggs, 1 tsp vanilla, 454 g chunky peanut butter, 2 2/3 cups (375 g) AP flour, 1 tsp baking soda, 1 tsp salt. One volume discrepancy worth flagging for the conversion project: the blog writes 454 g as '1 1/4 cups' where the family copy says '1 3/4 cups' - the family copy is the correct conversion (peanut butter runs about 256 g per cup), so trust the 454 g and the 1 3/4 cups. Confidence medium because this is an unaffiliated blog, not the publisher; the licensed cookbook text is behind a paywall at https://app.ckbk.com/recipe/flou69447c02s001r006/peanut-butter-cookies. Note also the blog bakes at 160C for 16 minutes against the family copy's 18-20 minutes.

name: General Tso's Chicken
flags: The family copy is the New York Times adaptation of Fuchsia Dunlop's Revolutionary Chinese Cookbook recipe - it is in US measures with NYT's numbered-step house style (12 ounces boneless skinless chicken thighs, 1 quart peanut oil for frying, potato starch with a corn starch alternative given in parentheses, 'Rice, for serving'), not Dunlop's own metric text, and Robert archived it on 2013-02-15 when that piece ran. cooking.nytimes.com returns SITE_BLOCKED, so no URL recorded and no digest built. Fuchsia Dunlop's own essay on the dish is at http://www.fuchsiadunlop.com/the-fabulous-general-tso/ (background, not the recipe); an unrelated version is at https://www.saveur.com/article/Recipes/Classic-General-Tso-Chicken - do not attach that one.

name: Pan-Fried Risotto
flags: No source line in the family copy, but it is a New York Times recipe: the ingredient list's '4 to 5 cups vegetable broth (see recipe)' cross-reference is NYT Cooking's own convention, the numbered steps and voice match David Tanis, and a reprint titled 'Pan-Fried Risotto Cakes' exists on The New York Times Wine Club. cooking.nytimes.com is SITE_BLOCKED, and the Wine Club mirror (https://www.nytwineclub.com/recipes/pan-fried-risotto-cakes) failed to fetch with a robots/DNS error rather than serving content - a human with NYT access should confirm the author and pull the digest.

name: Overnight White Bread
headnote: Ken Forkish's Overnight White Bread from Flour Water Salt Yeast. The whole formula turns on using almost no yeast - 0.8 g, eight hundredths of a percent of the flour - so that a 12-to-14-hour bulk ferment at room temperature does the leavening slowly and the dough's enzymes have time to build the nutty, faintly sweet flavour that normally only a sourdough gets. At 78 percent hydration the dough is slack, which is why it is mixed by hand with the pincer method rather than kneaded, and baked in a preheated covered Dutch oven so its own steam sets the crust.
comment_digest: NO COMMENTS on the page. Timings it records: 12-14 hours bulk at 70-72F, 60-75 minutes proof, bake 475F for 30 minutes covered then 15-20 minutes uncovered.
flags: Formula matches the family copy to the gram and to the baker's percentage: white flour 1,000 g / 100 percent; water at 90-95F (32-35C) 780 g / 78 percent; fine sea salt 22 g / 2.2 percent; instant dried yeast 0.8 g / 0.08 percent; two loaves of about 900 g (the family copy says about 1 1/2 lb each, same thing). The family copy's schedule - mix at 7 p.m., shape 8 a.m., bake 9:15 a.m. - is Forkish's own. This is a bread blog rather than the publisher; Forkish's own site (https://kensartisan.com/flour-water-salt-yeast) has the book page but not the formula. Useful cross-check with a halved version and a fuller method write-up: http://210degrees.blogspot.com/2013/10/overnight-white-bread-flour-water-salt.html (500 g flour, 390 g water, 11 g salt).

name: Saffron Chicken Thighs
flags: Identified with high confidence as Naz Deravian, Bottom of the Pot: Persian Recipes and Stories - it is the sibling of this batch's Everyday Turmeric Chicken, sharing her exact MAKE AHEAD / PLAN AHEAD blocks, the instruction to rinse the last of the saffron water out of the glass, and her signature closing line 'Taste and make delicious.' Robert's own forward even titled it 'Persian chicken thighs.' No online copy exists: kosher.com carries two Deravian recipes but not this one, and her site https://bottomofthepot.com/category/chicken/ does not host it. No link recorded rather than attach an unrelated saffron chicken. A human with the book can cite it directly.

name: Chocolate Banana Bread Pudding
flags: Source identified but no usable page. The recipe is Chocolate Banana Bread Pudding from Joanne Chang's Flour: Spectacular Recipes from Boston's Flour Bakery + Cafe - the family copy's gram-first ingredient list (170 g milk chocolate, 56 g semisweet, 100 g sugar, 1.4 kg half-and-half) is Chang's house style, and it was archived the same day (2014-02-12) as this batch's Flour Oatmeal Raisin Cookies. The licensed cookbook text is paywalled at https://app.ckbk.com/recipe/flou69447c05s001r006/chocolate-banana-bread-pudding (index confirmation at https://www.eatyourbooks.com/library/recipes/440499/chocolate-banana-bread-pudding), so no digest could be built. Two blog versions credited to Chang do NOT match the family copy and should not be promoted: https://littlegourmetblog.wordpress.com/2015/12/30/chocolate-banana-bread-pudding/ (7 yolks + 3 eggs, 1 cup sugar, bittersweet only, 10 cups bread) and https://www.jessiesheehanbakes.com/2015/06/03/chocolate-banana-bread-pudding/ (a different recipe entirely, built on homemade chocolate banana bread). Gram weights already in the family copy: milk chocolate 170 g, semisweet 56 g, half-and-half 6 cups = 1.4 kg, sugar 100 g.

name: Red-Braised Pork (Dunlop)
flags: Fuchsia Dunlop's red-braised pork, but not the version that circulates online. The family copy (1-1.25 lb pork belly with skin, 2 inches ginger, 2 scallions, 3 Tbsp peanut oil, 2 cups stock, 1 Tbsp dark soy, 2 Tbsp Shaoxing, 3/4 tsp salt, 3 Tbsp brown sugar, 1/2 star anise, simmered 2 hours) uses brown sugar and a stock-based braise with no cinnamon, which rules out the Every Grain of Rice version reprinted at https://wtfdoieattonight.com/2014/02/04/fuchsia-dunlops-red-braised-pork-recipe/ (500 g pork, 2 Tbsp caster sugar, cinnamon, 500 ml stock) and the Hunan hongshao rou this batch matched elsewhere. Likely Land of Plenty or Every Grain of Rice in a different printing. Not linked. Also note the library's own transcription flag: '3.4 tsp salt' in the ingredient list is almost certainly 3/4 tsp.

name: Leek And Potato Soup Or Vichyssoise
flags: Joy of Cooking, 1975 edition - a book recipe with no authorised online text. The family copy's tells are period-specific (poultry stock rather than chicken broth, optional mace, 'chipped' watercress or chives, the instruction to pare and slice the potatoes very fine, and the hot-or-cold framing), and no online version matches. Not to be confused with the collection's separate 'Leek and Potato Soup' by Pierre Franey, which already carries a source. Nothing worth promoting among the generic vichyssoise pages found.

name: Grilled Marinated Shrimp Skewers
flags: Searched on the exact marinade and could not match it. Family copy: 1 lb large shrimp, 3 Tbsp olive oil, 2 Tbsp lemon juice, 1/2 tsp salt, 1/4 tsp black pepper, 1 tsp oregano, 1/2 tsp paprika, 1/2 tsp garlic powder, 15 min to 2 hr marinade, 2-3 min per side. The dried-spice profile (oregano + paprika + garlic powder, no fresh garlic) is what fails to match. Candidates checked and rejected: https://www.dinneratthezoo.com/grilled-shrimp-skewers/ (1/4 cup oil, Italian seasoning, minced garlic; 5 stars, 99 votes - the closest in phrasing and the source of the 2-hour marinade cap, but a different spice list), https://www.dinneratthezoo.com/shrimp-marinade/ (honey, soy, thyme), https://thecookingfoodie.com/recipe/shrimp-skewers-baked-or-grilled/ (6 Tbsp oil, smoked paprika, fresh garlic). Note the library records that this entry's 2026 revision came from Claude conversations, not the archive, so part of the text may never have had a web source.

name: Chicken Sour Cream Enchiladas
flags: Family source - sent by Laura MacArthur to Robert, 2025-01-25, with her own two '(Laura added)' edits in the body and first-person brand preferences (La Victoria enchilada sauce, Mexican-blend cheese). One confirming search run; nothing published matches this combination of rotisserie chicken, a taco-seasoning packet toasted in oil, 1 cup sour cream, 1/2 cup parsley and 3 cups cheese. No link recorded.
